And the topic of today is what it takes to set intelligence free. And really for us this takes us back to when we started three years ago.

and really the UI was very similar to what it is today, where you kind of have a chat and in this preview. But the AI at that point was quite simple, we just had a prompt and response, one LLM call per user message.

spoken_segments.text: And so we thought, let's go out and build this agentic framework. And so we went and we built this very sophisticated, dare I say, beautiful framework for agents to work.
We had kind of this one main agent that would talk to the user and that agent would spawn other agents like an implementation agent here in the example.
And they would all talk to each other, send messages back and forth and we thought, wow, this is beautiful... and in the end it didn't work at all. It just made the product worse.

spoken_segments.text: And so I'll go into some of the things that we've done in our architecture to enable this. The first piece is really around the agent runtime itself...
The second piece is the computer, where each of these agents are actually doing their work...
The last piece then is the verification itself, where if you want an agent to work for a long amount of time, you need feedback loops.

scenes.screen_title: The agent runtime: Always-on
scenes.visual_summary: Agent Control Plane (ACP) architecture diagram showing Inbox queue aggregating external triggers into Task History trajectory.
ocr_details: Agent control plane (ACP) - Starts agents, and wakes one up when its inbox gets a message
Anyone can drop a message in the inbox. The agent copies it into its history between steps.
scenes.structured_reconstruction:
flowchart TD You["You (Human)"] --> Inbox Other["Other agents"] --> Inbox Sched["Scheduled wake-ups"] --> Inbox subgraph ACP ["Agent Control Plane (ACP)"] Inbox["Inbox: 'What's the status?'"] end Inbox --> Trajectory["Task history (trajectory)
[Request] -> [Tool call] -> [Result] -> [What's the status?] -> [Tool call]"]

spoken_segments.text: And so, if we start by looking at the agent runtime itself... you have three different sources that can interact with an agent: yourself, other agents, or a schedule.
For each agent we have a separate inbox where any of these sources send in messages.
The agent then can copy that itself into its own what we call a trajectory, basically its task history.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker points to the inbox node receiving async messages and copying them into task history.

scenes.screen_title: Fork the task history at any step
scenes.visual_summary: Tree graph showing history branching capability ('Rewrite it in Rust' fork extending off 'Read file' node).
ocr_details: Fork the task history at any step
Each event points to the one before it. A fork points to the same parent and copies nothing.
scenes.structured_reconstruction:
flowchart LR
    Main1["Improve performance"] --> Main2["Start"] --> Main3["Read file"]
    Main3 --> Fork1["Rewrite it in Rust"]
    Fork1 --> Fork2["Edit file"]
    Fork2 --> Fork3["Test: ok"]
    Fork3 --> Fork4["Done"]

spoken_segments.text: And we designed this trajectory with really Git as inspiration. It's an append-only log where each event points towards a parent...
Because of this, you get a nice capability just like in Git where you can fork things, right?
Unlike Git, we cannot merge agent trajectories, but we can kind of spawn them out.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker gestures along the blue forked branch on screen.

spoken_segments.text: Then what we've done is to make sure that we have this append-only log, and from that we can actually build a prompt that we would feed into the actual LLM.
When you build a prompt... if you have a long history, you probably want to do some sort of compaction and summarize part of that history.
By separating the prompt from the actual task history, we're able to render prompts for any type of model or task.

spoken_segments.text: And then the question is, why do we care about this? Well, at Lovable, we deploy to this system 700 times per day. So that's about once every 2 minutes.
And you can imagine if you have an agent working for 10 hours... you want to not disrupt that agent when it's working.
We can actually make sure that we have one agent working on one task but we can have different processes taking up and actually doing the compute.

spoken_segments.text: And so we've had to do some optimizations to make this feasible to actually run. One of these optimizations is copy-on-write on the RAM itself.
as soon as you start writing in a process to RAM, we will kind of copy that page over and only then will you start having to allocate new memory.

scenes.screen_title: Two loops: fix it now, improve it later
scenes.visual_summary: Comprehensive comparative table detailing Inner Loop checks (turn-time fixes) vs Outer Loop checks (horizon business metrics).
ocr_details: Two loops: fix it now, improve it later
The agent sees it and fixes it right away
The horizon between turns is long
Production outcomes reach the agent only as next-turn findings, never as a training signal.
scenes.structured_reconstruction:
| Inner Loop (During turn) | Type | Outer Loop (Between turns) | Type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Build, lint + type errors | Automatic | Production signals | Automatic |
| Runtime errors | Automatic + tools | Visitor behaviour | Automatic |
| Browser + visual checks | Tools | What users tell you | Explicit |
| Judges in the turn | Automatic | Automatic A/B tests | Automatic |
| Domain scanners | Tools | Transactions -> conversions | Automatic |
| Backend logs + usage | Tools | Feedbacks fed back | Next turn |
| Guardrails + notifications | Automatic | | |
| User-triggered fixes | User | | |

spoken_segments.text: If you look at verification, you can think of these feedback loops... this inner loop and this outer loop.
This inner loop is during the turn of the agent: build, lint errors, type errors, runtime errors, headless browser.
Then you also have this outer loop between each turn... product metrics, visitor behavior, AB tests, business metrics.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker walks down both columns comparing real-time inner turn checks against production outer loop feedback signals.
